title: Stress Reset: Physiological Sighs
description: Your ring has spent a large part of today with an elevated heart rate while you were sitting still, which is a pattern that often goes with stress. A few minutes of physiological sighs is a fast, low-effort way to bring arousal back down.
source: Huberman Lab (physiological sigh / cyclic sighing); Balban et al. 2023, Cell Reports Medicine; experimental daytime-stress trigger

all.label: 60+ minutes of stillness with a raised heart rate today (phone-estimated)
45+ minutes of stillness with a raised heart rate today (phone-estimated)
last night's HRV < 90% of rolling baseline

conditional.question: Your ring shows a lot of time today with a raised heart rate while you were still. Does that match how today has felt?

actions.frequency: Up to 3 times today, when tension is highest
actions.timing: Whenever you notice tension; good before a meeting or after a stressful exchange
actions.details: Inhale deeply through the nose, then take a second short sniff on top to fully inflate the lungs, then exhale slowly and completely through the mouth. Repeat for 1-5 minutes. The long exhale is the part that slows the heart rate.

actions.action: Step outside for a short walk
actions.frequency: Once, on the day this triggers
actions.timing: Any time, ideally away from screens
actions.details: Walk at an easy pace and let your gaze rest on the horizon instead of a screen. Low-intensity movement with a wide visual field is a simple way to lower arousal without adding training stress.

benefits: Quickly lowers physiological arousal without needing equipment or time set aside
Breathing with an emphasis on the exhale is associated with a calmer heart rate and better mood
Gives a concrete response to a stress signal instead of just noticing it
science: A controlled study found that five minutes a day of cyclic sighing (long-exhale breathing) improved mood and reduced resting respiratory rate more than mindfulness meditation over a month, and Huberman describes the physiological sigh as the fastest real-time tool for lowering stress. This rule is experimental: the stress estimate comes from heart rate relative to your own resting rate while you are still, and is computed on your phone rather than being a validated measure of stress.
contraindications: Stop and breathe normally if you feel lightheaded
The stress estimate is approximate and can be raised by caffeine, illness, or dehydration as well as stress
If you feel persistently anxious or unwell, talk to a doctor or mental health professional rather than relying on an app estimate

How to Breathe Correctly for Optimal Health, Mood, Learning & Performance — Huberman Lab

evidence_metadata.scientific_rationale: Heart rate elevated above the personal resting rate during stillness, sustained for an hour, is a reasonable proxy for sympathetic arousal without physical cause. The second group adds a low overnight HRV as corroboration so the lower 45-minute threshold still requires a second signal.

evidence_for_protocol.notes: Cyclic sighing for five minutes a day reduced anxiety and improved mood in a randomized study (Balban et al., Cell Reports Medicine, 2023), and the physiological sigh is a standard Huberman Lab stress tool.

evidence_for_trigger.notes: The 60 and 45 minute cutoffs and the +15 bpm above-resting definition are first-pass guesses and have not been tuned on a full day of real ring data. Coverage is limited because the ring only reports clean heartbeats when you are still. Treat as unvalidated until tuned against real outcomes.

expected_effect.short_term: A few minutes of long-exhale breathing should lower heart rate and subjective tension within the session.
expected_effect.long_term: Responding to early stress signals with a brief reset may reduce accumulated daytime arousal, though this specific trigger has not been outcome-tested.
